questions.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression for Flux
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068094/assets/b37c10064003374c146c58bba99ff55304529ee66c9fb38c44246ccc90e8f402.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and the square $C$ with side length $4$ centered at $O,$ shown above. If the flux of $F$ across the side ${C}_{1}$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}\boxed{}\,\text{d}s,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

In our case, we need to find an expression for the flux across only the part ${C}_{1}$ of the closed curve $C.$ Since this side is perpendicular to the $x$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have $n=i.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068094/assets/c4c4f2f3d5b6188ac5a6ec41bb96fc0c7132cc39308cebfa16ee759eabac2c75.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}({x}^{2}\,i+{y}^{2}\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}s\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${x}^{2}.$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{3}y\,i-x{y}^{2}\,j$ and the rectangle $C,$ shown above. If the flux of $F$ across the side ${C}_{3}$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{3}}\boxed{}\,\text{d}s,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

In our case, we need to find an expression for the flux across only the part ${C}_{3}$ of the closed curve $C.$ Since this side is perpendicular to the $x$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have $n=-i.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068094/assets/c6dd493e02633854184be1be0f38246e1e9dce2949f9cc1aa93b943c91d1e44c.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{3}}({x}^{3}y\,i-x{y}^{2}\,j)\cdot (-i)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{3}}-{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}s\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is $-{x}^{3}y.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Flux Across a Square Using Symmetry
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068094/assets/6f827dac7ecaf3a659245d1178aa39a519ae3a40339c917004247f12554c871a.png)

Consider the vector field $F=2x\,i+2y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $8$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068094/assets/0b753318ebad9270c3fc8788d0e3949ffb29a800eb3f8dd6fb67cb271be68033.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\,i+2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=4\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-4,4].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-4}^{4}4\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-4}^{4}\text{d}t \\  & =8(4-(-4)) \\  & =8\cdot 8 \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot 64=256.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Flux Across a Rectangle Using Two Symmetry Properties
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068094/assets/2dcfb8778adf7e9a05ff1dff886d0d8290427ed2ae910b46db4fe9aeb36170eb.png)

Consider the vector field $F=x\,i+3y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068094/assets/f283fe675e0a9ef736947e404f03ab5afb90a4209ba1a6949d18ac6d3fb20048.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(x\,i+3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=3\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =3\cdot 6 \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=18.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(x\,i+3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+3\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =9\cdot 6 \\  & =54.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=54.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 18+2\cdot 54=144.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068094/assets/80cc5e165f78bc1fc8cc7f83644fd00ca4a8f4e05e69d97b654bb2f1450d9b99.png)

Consider the vector field $F=-x\,i+3y\,j$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $6$ and height $4$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068094/assets/511bae61d710c3362bb18618717b3d44ef5dcedece5f669e0b5237b7b524a054.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-x\,i+3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=3i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-{\int }_{-2}^{2}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 4 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=-12.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(-x\,i+3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+2\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot 6 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=36.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot (-12)+2\cdot 36=48.
$$
